source.title: Renormalizable Spectral-Shell Dynamics as the Origin of Neural Scaling Laws

record.file_problem: The full paper is present and readable. Some equations have minor text-extraction artifacts, but the relevant content is intact.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws and proposes a theoretical explanation, but it does not measure the loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute relationships, predict larger-run losses, or test compute-optimal allocation. Its experiments measure spectral-shell error profiles instead.
record.gate_note: The paper reports empirical spectral-shell measurements on Pythia checkpoints, not results on any listed scaling-law version. The shell-profile findings are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. Its scaling-law discussion and cited results are not additional rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a theory meant to explain neural scaling laws and double descent. It reports no measurement of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It does no extrapolation, compute-allocation sweep, shape comparison, other-modality fit or downstream evaluation. Its only experiments measure spectral-shell profiles of squared log-probability error on Pythia checkpoints. That is a different construct, and the authors say it is not for fitting scaling exponents. The power-law loss in time, L(t) ∝ t^-((1+c0)p+1), is derived from assumed effective power-law transport and is never fitted to data.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors derive a renormalizable spectral-shell framework that, under an assumed effective power-law transport, explains scaling laws and double descent. They present the Pythia experiments as evidence that the assumed shell structures exist, not as fits of scaling exponents.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a theoretical spectral-shell framework and measures spectral-shell error profiles; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law sweeps or their loss-versus-scale fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported spectral profiles change across training checkpoints: the peak shifts toward smaller λ and the high-resolution tail contracts. The cross-model comparison reports differences in overall energy scale and peak location between Pythia 70M and 7B.

fits_no_version.finding: Squared log-probability error in Pythia checkpoints has a unimodal log-shell energy profile with a sharp high-resolution cutoff. The peak shifts to smaller λ over training (1k to 8k steps), and the coarse structure is similar for Pythia 70M and 7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM error spectra under the Jacobian-induced operator show a structured shell profile with a moving resolution frontier that persists across model scales.

record.problems: The empirical section does not fit or predict scaling-law exponents and reports qualitative shell-profile descriptions rather than numerical comparisons. It analyzes only Pythia 70M, 410M, and 7B checkpoints, while the displayed cross-model comparison is 70M versus 7B. The paper also states that the renormalizable flux interface and effective power-law transport are assumptions; its empirical error observable is squared log-probability, justified by a local approximation.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported results left out. Pythia 410M is listed among analyzed models, but the text gives no separate outcome for it.

untested.parts: No loss-versus-parameters, tokens or compute measurements; the time-scaling law is derived theoretically, not measured.
No fits on small runs or predictions for larger runs.
No comparison of architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
No exponent or allocation fit-dependence is measured. The reported cutoff concerns shell energy versus spectral resolution, not loss versus scale.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The scaling-law form appears only as a theoretical consequence of assumptions, and the authors say the renormalizability and power-law transport are assumed. The empirical observable is squared log-probability error, justified only by a local quadratic approximation. All results are qualitative and come with no uncertainty estimates. Pythia 410M is listed among the analysed models but no result is reported for it.

versions.untested_parts: No loss scaling against parameter count, training tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or predictions for larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or optimal parameter/token scaling is measured.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
No other modality or training-regime scaling law is tested.
No downstream-task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss is tested.

The paper does not test scaling-law exponent or allocation fit-dependence, or whether loss-versus-scale curves bend away from a power law. Its reported bend/cutoff concerns spectral-shell energy versus spectral resolution, a different quantity.

rows.subject: Pythia 7B
rows.operation_detail: Estimated squared log-probability error energy in logarithmic spectral shells using stochastic Lanczos.

conditions.value: approximately 50 batches, each 128 context windows with batch size 4; roughly 2.5 × 10^5 tokens total

rows.measure: Log-shell energy profile across spectral resolutions
rows.value: The profile is unimodal; its low-resolution side is approximately affine in log–log coordinates, and the minimum shell energy collapses to a numerical floor past a finite resolution. The text describes that high-resolution cutoff as incompatible with an extended power-law tail.
rows.note: This is a spectral-shell profile, not held-out loss as a function of model size, tokens, or compute.

rows.subject: Pythia model (size not stated for Figure 2)
rows.operation_detail: Compared log-shell error-energy profiles across training checkpoints.
rows.measure: Log-shell energy profile across spectral resolutions
rows.value: The checkpoint profiles are described as unimodal; across training, the spectral peak moves toward smaller λ and the high-resolution tail contracts. Low-λ profiles remain approximately parallel in log–log coordinates while their amplitudes increase.
rows.note: The discussion reports an aggregate pattern across the plotted checkpoints, not a separate numerical result for this checkpoint.

relation.reason: The paper develops an explanatory framework for scaling laws. Section 7 explicitly distinguishes its structural measurements from fitting scaling exponents.

tranche.reason: The empirical results measure spectral-shell organization, not any claim version's loss-versus-scale relationship. The conditional theoretical derivation explains scaling under assumed transport rather than independently testing the listed versions.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased: renormalizability and effective power-law transport remain assumptions. The supplied text is arXiv v5 dated 8 January 2026; the pack lists publication year 2025.
